6
A ball is kicked upwards at an angle of 45° to horizontal ground. After a short flight, the ball
returns to the ground.
It may be assumed that air resistance is negligible.
What is never zero during the flight of the ball?
A
the horizontal component of the ball’s acceleration
B
the horizontal component of the ball’s velocity
C
the vertical component of the ball’s momentum
D
the vertical component of the ball’s velocity

hints: Notice the ball is launched at $45^\circ$, so it starts with both a horizontal component $u \cos 45^\circ$ and a vertical component $u \sin 45^\circ$.
With air resistance negligible, there is no horizontal force so horizontal acceleration is zero, while vertical motion has acceleration $g$ downwards.
Check what happens at maximum height: the vertical component of velocity momentarily becomes zero, so test which listed quantity can avoid being zero there.
walkthrough: Resolve the launch: initial horizontal velocity is $u_x = u \cos 45^\circ$ and initial vertical velocity is $u_y = u \sin 45^\circ$, both non-zero.
Use the force rule with negligible air resistance: the only force is weight vertically downwards, so $a_x = 0$ and $a_y = -g$.
Apply this to horizontal motion: because $a_x = 0$, $v_x$ remains constant at $u \cos 45^\circ$ throughout the flight and never becomes zero.
Apply this to vertical motion: $v_y = u \sin 45^\circ - gt$ decreases, is zero at the highest point, then becomes negative.
Since vertical momentum is $m v_y$, it is also zero when $v_y$ is zero at the top, and horizontal acceleration is always zero.
Therefore only the horizontal component of velocity is never zero. This is option B

A.explanation: With no air resistance there is no horizontal force, so horizontal acceleration is always zero, not never zero.

B.explanation: With no air resistance horizontal velocity stays constant at $u \cos 45^\circ$, which is non-zero for the whole flight.

C.explanation: Vertical momentum is $m v_y$ and $v_y$ is zero at maximum height, so it is zero once during flight.

D.explanation: Vertical velocity decreases to zero at the top of the trajectory before becoming negative on the way down.
